prompt: What is the “cloning” critique of person-organisation fit in the theory video?

options.text: Firms copy job descriptions from competitors
If “fit” means “people like us”, firms hire the same profile again and again – diversity falls
Candidates copy each other's CVs
Firms re-hire former employees

explanation: The video flags that P-O fit can reduce diversity – the link to Lecture 3 on cultural fit and inequality.

prompt: Why can a heavy reliance on referrals (word-of-mouth) work against diversity?

options.text: Referrals are more expensive than open searches
Employees tend to refer people from their own networks – social capital and in-group favouritism reproduce the current workforce
Referred candidates are legally protected
Referrals attract too many unsuitable applications

explanation: Closed searches draw on existing networks (Bourdieu's social capital); in-group favouritism constrains diversity (Bell, 2013).

prompt: How does the theory-video summary rate references as a selection method?

options.text: Highly valid and reliable
Former employers' views with usually low validity
The most practicable method for senior roles
Illegal in most EU countries

explanation: References are cheap but tend to be positive and unspecific – low validity.

prompt: Why are structured interviews recommended both for validity/reliability and for reducing bias?

options.text: They are shorter than free conversations
Every candidate gets the same job-related questions, scored against criteria set in advance
They let the interviewer follow his or her gut feeling
They replace the need for a job analysis

explanation: Standardised, job-related questions and scoring make interviews more valid and reliable – and limit halo, horns and similar-to-me effects.

prompt: Which statement about tests as a selection method is NOT in line with the video summary?

options.text: They can measure ability, personality or skills
They are cheap and standardised
Personality tests can be faked
They are always more valid than probationary periods

explanation: Probationary periods observe real work and are very valid – but costly if the hire fails.

prompt: What risk does the video summary attach to innovative selection methods such as AI screening?

options.text: They are too slow
Bias risk
They can only be used for senior roles
They violate reliability by design

explanation: AI screening can reproduce historical bias – compare “algorithmically biased recruitment” as a sin of commission (Session 1).

prompt: A firm screens CVs mainly on university prestige. Using the video's criteria, what is the main concern?

options.text: Practicability – CV screening is too expensive
Validity – prestige may not predict performance in the job
Reliability – CVs cannot be read twice
None – prestige is a perfect predictor

explanation: The question is whether the signal measures what predicts job performance. Lecture 3 adds that such signals are partly produced by class origins.

prompt: What is a meritocratic system?

options.text: A system in which actors are rewarded for their talent and hard work
A system in which riches and rule are inherited
A system in which all employees earn the same
A system in which seniority decides promotion

explanation: In a meritocracy, riches and rule are earned, not inherited; power and privilege are allocated by individual merit, not social background.

prompt: Which formula summarises merit in the lecture?

options.text: IQ + Effort = Merit
Education × Experience = Merit
Talent − Luck = Merit
Signals + Networks = Merit

explanation: IQ + Effort = Merit – a promise that Ingram (2021) questions: what looks like merit is partly produced by class origins.

prompt: In Bourdieu's theory (as used by Ingram, 2021), what is SOCIAL capital?

options.text: Command over financial resources
Resources based on group membership, relations and networks of influence and support
Knowledge, skills and education
The prestige of an employer

explanation: Economic = money and assets; social = networks; cultural = knowledge, skills, education and expectations.

prompt: A candidate could afford several unpaid internships in London thanks to family money. Which capital mainly explains this CV entry?

options.text: Economic capital
Social capital
Cultural capital
Human capital

explanation: Financial resources (economic capital) made the unpaid internships possible – the signal is produced by money, not only ability.

prompt: A candidate interviews with confidence and “polish” and has high expectations of his career because his parents are academics. Which capital is this?

options.text: Economic capital
Social capital
Cultural capital
Signalling capital

explanation: Cultural capital: forms of knowledge, skills, education and any advantages giving higher standing, including high expectations.

prompt: Which of these is NOT a reason given by Baron & Kreps (1999) for relying on signals such as degrees?

options.text: Signals are expensive to obtain
They are granted by institutions that screen the candidate pool
Their acquisition requires acquiring knowledge
They are free of bias

explanation: The lecture adds: “But careful: signals can be biased!”

prompt: What is the HR challenge that the “Spoiled for choice” case illustrates?

options.text: Ignoring all signals on a CV
Distinguishing the signal from the underlying job-relevant capability
Hiring only candidates from top schools
Reading the evidence on the CV literally

explanation: “Evidence-based” selection is not the same as reading the evidence literally – weigh signals once you know how they were produced.

prompt: In “Spoiled for choice”, why might a prestige-oriented CV screen undervalue Peter?

options.text: Peter has no work experience
His experiences may reveal capabilities (e.g. responsibility, resilience, work experience) that conventional prestige signals do not capture
Peter does not fit EIC's culture
Peter's CV contains false information

explanation: The case asks which skills Peter may have acquired that John did not – and why a standard screen misses them.

prompt: According to the lecture, can the search for “fit” reproduce inequality?

options.text: No – fit is always a neutral criterion
Yes – the problem is how cultural fit is defined and assessed
Only in public organisations
Only if the firm uses open searches

explanation: Fit judged as “like us” turns into similar-to-me bias and reproduces homogeneity.

prompt: Which definition is correct?

options.text: Inequality: a cognitive or attitudinal process
Discrimination: differential treatment associated with group membership
Bias: unequal outcomes between groups
All three terms are interchangeable

explanation: Inequality = unequal outcomes; discrimination = differential treatment; bias = a cognitive/attitudinal process. Related, but NOT interchangeable.

prompt: A firm hires women less often than men. What can you conclude from this observation alone?

options.text: The firm discriminates against women
There is inequality in outcomes – discrimination is not yet proven
Recruiters are biased
The firm's selection methods are invalid

explanation: An outcome gap is inequality. To show discrimination you must rule out differences between candidates – e.g. with a field experiment.

prompt: An interviewer is impressed by a candidate's top-school degree and then rates everything else about the candidate positively. Which bias is this?

options.text: Horns effect
Halo effect
Self-delusion
Stereotyping

explanation: Halo effect: one positive feature → only positives are seen. The horns effect is the negative version.

prompt: A manager says: “I'm completely objective, bias is not an issue for me.” Which bias does Weston & Woods call this?

options.text: Similar-to-me
Self-delusion
Halo effect
In-group favouritism

explanation: Self-delusion: believing oneself immune from bias – remedy: training and monitoring data.

prompt: An interviewer treats himself as the “gold standard” and prefers candidates with his own background. Which bias, and which remedy fits best?

options.text: Similar-to-me – diverse interview panels
Halo effect – longer interviews
Stereotyping – more references
Horns effect – fewer criteria

explanation: Similar-to-me bias is reduced by involving a variety of actors, e.g. diverse panels.

prompt: What does the surgeon riddle (“I cannot operate on this boy, he is my son”) illustrate?

options.text: Halo effect
Unconscious gender stereotypes – many do not think of the doctor being his mother
Self-selection
Signalling theory

explanation: The doctor is the boy's mother; the difficulty shows unconscious gender stereotypes.

prompt: Which of these is NOT a mechanism of unconscious bias in R&S named in the lecture?

options.text: Gendered wording in job ads (Gaucher et al., 2011)
In-group favouritism (Bell, 2013)
Conformity to standardised approaches screening out neurodiverse people (Austin & Pisano, 2017)
Self-selection after a realistic job preview

explanation: Self-selection is a selection method from the theory video, not a bias mechanism.

prompt: Austin & Pisano (2017) argue that conventional R&S methods screen out neurodiverse people. What follows for selection design?

options.text: Standardisation should be abolished
Standardisation helps reliability, but the process must allow reasonable adjustments
Neurodiverse candidates should be hired without selection
Only interviews should be used

explanation: Absolute conformity to standard approaches excludes some talent – keep structure but allow adjustments.

prompt: How do the field experiments in Quillian et al.'s (2019) meta-analysis measure discrimination?

options.text: By comparing the hiring rates of real applicants
By sending applications that are equivalent in job-relevant characteristics and vary only racial/ethnic cues such as names
By interviewing recruiters about their attitudes
By analysing firms' diversity reports

explanation: Only the cue differs, so a callback gap can be causally attributed to discrimination.

prompt: What does the field-experiment design allow us to say that comparing real applicants cannot?

options.text: That candidates differ in qualifications
That the callback gap is caused by the group cue – causal inference
That discrimination is illegal
That recruiters are aware of their bias

explanation: Real applicants differ in many ways; equivalent constructed applications isolate the effect of the cue.

prompt: How is the discrimination ratio defined in Quillian et al. (2019)?

options.text: Callback rate of the target group / callback rate of white natives
Callback rate of white natives / callback rate of the target group
Share of minority employees in the firm
Number of applications / number of hires

explanation: A ratio above 1 means white natives receive more callbacks than the target group.

prompt: How many field experiments does the Quillian et al. (2019) meta-analysis cover?
explanation: 97 field experiments with more than 200,000 job applications in nine countries in Europe and North America.

prompt: Which finding of Mohammadi, Broström & Franzoni (2017) is correct?

options.text: Ethnic diversity can be replaced by collaborating with external partners
Disciplinary diversity can be substituted by intense collaboration with external partners
Ethnic diversity mainly facilitates incremental innovation
Diversity has no link with innovation

explanation: Disciplinary diversity can be substituted by external collaboration and helps radical and incremental innovation; ethnic diversity can neither be replaced nor complemented and mainly facilitates radical innovation.

basis.ref: Why reduce bias and increase diversity? (Mohammadi et al., 2017)

prompt: Which of these is NOT a core idea of an inclusive recruitment and selection process in the lecture?

options.text: Systematic and transparent criteria
Putting standard signals and preconceptions into question
Involving a variety of actors
Relying on the hiring manager's gut feeling about fit

explanation: Gut feeling about fit is exactly what produces similar-to-me bias; criteria should be set in advance and linked to the job.
